title: Decorator
summary: Add behavior by wrapping an object while keeping the same interface.

parts.rule: Decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped component and forwards calls, adding work before or after. Wrappers compose: logging plus compression plus encryption can stack. The client still programs to the original interface.
parts.why: Subclass explosions for every feature combination do not scale. Decorators mix features at runtime. Order of wrapping matters and must be intentional.
parts.example: Notifier interface with EmailNotifier. Wrapped as SmsDecorator(EmailNotifier) then SlackDecorator around that. On notify("down") once; 3 decorators fire in order, SlackDecorator posts, then SmsDecorator texts, then EmailNotifier emails. Another stack: InputStream read through BufferedDecorator then GZipDecorator. Client code still calls read on the outer decorator. Changing order changes behavior: encrypt-then-compress differs from compress-then-encrypt. Prefer decorator over subclassing when combinations are open-ended. body:
Rule. Decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped component and forwards calls, adding work before or after. Wrappers compose: logging plus compression plus encryption can stack. The client still programs to the original interface.

Why it matters. Subclass explosions for every feature combination do not scale. Decorators mix features at runtime. Order of wrapping matters and must be intentional.

Worked example. Notifier interface with EmailNotifier. Wrapped as SmsDecorator(EmailNotifier) then SlackDecorator around that. On notify("down") once; 3 decorators fire in order, SlackDecorator posts, then SmsDecorator texts, then EmailNotifier emails. Another stack: InputStream read through BufferedDecorator then GZipDecorator. Client code still calls read on the outer decorator. Changing order changes behavior: encrypt-then-compress differs from compress-then-encrypt. Prefer decorator over subclassing when combinations are open-ended. When to use. Use decorators for cross-cutting add-ons: logging, metrics, caching, authz checks, compression. Use them when feature combinations should be chosen at composition time.

When to refuse. Refuse decorators that change the interface contract in surprising ways. Refuse deep stacks no one can debug. Refuse decorator when a single subclass or a strategy swap is clearer. Refuse putting core business branching only inside decorators that obscure the main path.
